summary: This informational document establishes a common understanding of baseline scenarios for evaluating different information-centric networking (ICN) approaches, so they can be tested and compared against each other.

plainLanguage.summary: Some researchers want the internet to fetch things by what they are rather than where they are. This lists test situations so the different ideas can be compared fairly.

subtitle: Reference scenarios to fairly compare different information-centric network designs.

tldr.problem: Information-centric networking (ICN) is a new research direction where the network fetches content by name rather than by host address, but different ICN proposals exist and there is no agreed way to compare them fairly.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys peer-reviewed ICN literature and identifies nine baseline scenarios—social networking, real-time communication, mobile networking, and others—where different ICN architectures can be tested side by side using the same methodology and metrics.
tldr.outcome: Researchers have a common reference framework for evaluating their ICN proposals and comparing results with other approaches, accelerating progress on the most promising designs.

today: RFC 7476 is an Informational RFC that remains relevant to ICN research. It has not been obsoleted and continues to serve as a reference for baseline scenarios in ICN evaluations.

sections.title: Information-Centric Networking and the Need for Baselines
sections.content:
The Internet today is built on a host-centric model: you connect to a specific server (identified by its IP address) to fetch data. Information-centric networking (ICN) inverts this: instead of asking "where is the data?", you ask "what is this data?", and the network finds and delivers it from whoever has a copy.

This shift enables powerful new capabilities: content can be cached anywhere in the network, mobility is handled natively (you move but your request still finds the content), and multicast and broadcast work as first-class primitives. Multiple ICN architectures have been proposed, including Content-Centric Networking (CCN), Named Data Networking (NDN), NetInf, and others. Each claims advantages, but without a common framework for testing, comparing their claims is difficult.

This document establishes baseline scenarios—test setups and workloads—so that different ICN proposals can be evaluated fairly and their results compared on an equal footing.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of "give me what's on server 192.168.1.5", ICN lets you say "give me the news", and the network finds it. But there are many ways to build this, and we need common tests to see which works best.

sections.title: Nine Evaluation Scenarios
sections.content:
The document identifies nine categories of use cases where ICN might excel:

Social Networking: Users share content with friends and followers without needing centralized servers. ICN's multicast and caching let one post reach many recipients efficiently.

Real-Time Communication: Audio and video calls, conferences, and multiplayer games. ICN can reduce latency and improve scalability for these stringent QoS requirements.

Mobile Networking: Devices move between networks, switching between cellular and WiFi. ICN's location-independent naming avoids the complexity of anchor-based mobility protocols like Mobile IP.

Infrastructure Sharing: Edge devices contribute storage and bandwidth to the network. ICN's security model (securing the data itself, not the channel) enables secure peer-to-peer sharing at unprecedented scale.

Content Dissemination: Video streaming, file distribution, mirroring, and bulk transfers. These are ICN's heartland; caching and native multicast offer efficiency gains over IP-based CDNs.

Vehicular Networking: Cars and roadside units communicate intermittently and opportunistically. ICN's tolerance for disruption suits highly mobile environments.

Delay and Disruption Tolerance: Networks with intermittent connectivity, such as disaster-recovery scenarios or remote areas. ICN's in-network caching allows messages to hop forward even when endpoints are offline.

Internet of Things: Billions of devices, each producing small amounts of data. ICN's efficient multicast and caching help aggregate and distribute sensor data at scale.

Smart City: Coordinated services (traffic lights, emergency response, environmental monitoring) communicating over a shared network. ICN's ability to decouple producers and consumers aids this coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Social media needs multicast, calls need low latency, phones move between networks, cars drive in and out of coverage, sensors produce lots of small data—nine situations where ICN might be better than IP.

sections.title: Challenges Spanning All Scenarios
sections.content:
Beyond individual scenarios, the document identifies three cross-cutting concerns:

Multiply Connected Nodes: Many devices now have multiple network interfaces (WiFi and cellular, for example). Economists argue that the cost of providing multiple paths to a node can be substantial. ICN proposals must address whether and how they support multi-homed nodes efficiently, and what incentive structures allow users and networks to share the cost.

Energy Efficiency: Wireless networks, IoT devices, and mobile gadgets are battery-constrained. ICN can theoretically reduce energy by caching content locally and avoiding repeated transmission. However, the cost of name-based lookups, in-network computation, and opportunistic forwarding must be carefully evaluated. Different ICN approaches make different energy trade-offs.

Operation Across Multiple Network Paradigms: The real Internet mixes wired and wireless, fixed and mobile, overlay and underlay. ICN solutions must interoperate with IP networks and other technologies, not just run in isolation. Evaluations should include scenarios where ICN islands exist within a larger IP-based Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones have WiFi and cellular, batteries can't last forever, and the real internet is messy. Any real ICN design has to handle all three.

sections.title: Metrics and Evaluation Methodology
sections.content:
The document summarizes the aspects that ICN evaluation should measure: network efficiency (bandwidth, latency, throughput), reduced complexity (fewer protocols, simpler state management), increased scalability (handling more users or content), reliability (resilience to failures), mobility support (seamless handovers), multicast and caching performance (reducing redundant traffic), real-time communication efficiency (meeting QoS/QoE targets), energy consumption, disruption and delay tolerance, information security and trust, persistence (surviving server failures), availability (findability), provenance (tracing content origin), and location independence.

Separate work (referenced but not included here) details the methodology for how to run these evaluations—which traffic patterns to use, which topologies to simulate, which metrics to report, and how to ensure results are reproducible.

The document notes that in the late 1970s, different packet-switched technologies (IP, IPX, DECnet) were being developed in parallel. ICN is in a similar position today. Baseline scenarios are a step toward maturing the field so the best ideas can emerge.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements matter: how fast, how far, how much data, how much power, can you trust the content. The document lists what to measure and why, so everyone compares apples to apples.

sections.title: Scope and Future Work
sections.content:
RFC 7476 is informational; it does not propose a standard and does not mandate that all ICN research follow these scenarios. Rather, it is a consensus view of what the Information-Centric Networking Research Group of the IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) has learned from surveying the literature. The hope is to provide enough detail and reference material that researchers can adopt these scenarios, implement them, and produce comparable results.

The document acknowledges that ICN research is still young and rapidly evolving. Different approaches will continue to emphasize different scenarios—that is healthy at this stage. However, as the field matures, a shared evaluation framework helps identify which ideas are most promising and accelerates convergence toward deployable solutions.

Mobile networking scenarios have been underdeveloped relative to others; future work should focus more on how ICN handles moving sources, not just moving consumers. Similarly, the interplay between ICN security (data-object integrity) and privacy needs more attention. These gaps point to important areas for future research.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a research roadmap, not a rule. It says, "Here are nine things worth testing, and here's why." Researchers are free to build and test their own scenarios too, but having common ground helps.
